Thesis · Chapter 5 · Thermal simulation

A digital twin of a printed thermoelectric generator

A thermoelectric generator converts only the temperature difference that reaches its legs, so designing one is a thermal-management problem. I built a finite-element (FEA) model of a fully screen-printed organic generator in COMSOL Multiphysics, validated it against the measured devices, and used it as a digital twin: to see where the heat goes, why the textbook model fails for thin printed devices, and which design changes could win back three orders of magnitude of power.

01 · The hardware

Five printed layers on 25 µm of plastic

The device being twinned is a vertical (Π-type) thermoelectric generator made entirely by screen printing, on an industrial printer at room temperature. On a 25 µm Kapton film go, in order: silver bottom contacts (3 µm), a dielectric layer with cylindrical wells, a p-type ink filling half the wells, silver filling the other half, and silver top contacts (3 µm). Air-stable, printable n-type inks are still scarce, so silver legs stand in for the n-type ones: the generator is unipolar. Two p-type inks went through the same process, a commercial PEDOT:PSS and an additive-free graphene ink.

Devices with 4, 8 and 800 thermocouples (0.5, 1 and 100 cm²) were measured under temperature differences of 5 to 25 K while sweeping the load, and all of them follow the ideal load curve. The 8-thermocouple graphene device delivers the most: 15 nW at ΔT = 29.5 K. Normalized by area and ΔT2, that is the highest power density reported among fully printed vertical OTEGs.

The device is light (1 µW g-1), its resistance does not change when bent to a 1 cm radius, and the process scales: the same layout was printed as a 10 × 10 cm² generator with 800 thermocouples. Still, it makes nanowatts out of a 25-kelvin difference. The question for the model is where that difference goes.

02 · FEA model

Microns thick, centimetres wide

Printing devices is slow and expensive; simulating them is not. I rebuilt the 8-thermocouple device in COMSOL Multiphysics as a full 3D model: heat transfer in solids coupled to electric currents, with the temperature field driving the current through the Seebeck effect. The inputs are the properties measured on the printed films. The boundary conditions replicate the bench: the bottom of the substrate is held at 298 K + ΔT and the top at 298 K, one terminal is grounded, and the other is either left open, for the open-circuit voltage, or swept through applied potentials, for the internal resistance and the power.

The hard part is the geometry. The layers are 3 to 25 µm thick and the device is a centimetre across, aspect ratios above a thousand to one, which free tetrahedra handle badly. The mesh is swept instead: triangles on the top faces, extruded in layers through the thickness, densest in the thin printed layer. Refining it does not change the results.

ToolCOMSOL Multiphysics, finite elements
PhysicsHeat transfer in solids and electric currents, coupled by the Seebeck effect
Geometry3D, 8 thermocouples: substrate 25 µm, legs 9 µm, interconnects 3 µm
InputsMeasured σ, S and κ of each printed material (below)
BoundariesSubstrate bottom at 298 K + ΔT, top at 298 K; one terminal grounded, the other open or swept
MeshSwept, layered through the thickness; results independent of mesh size
Left outConvection, radiation, Peltier and Joule heating

03 · Validation

A twin that agrees with the bench, and flags where it doesn't

A model only becomes a digital twin once it reproduces the real device. The simulated VOC matches the measurements within ~6% for PEDOT:PSS. For graphene it is within ~27%, probably because the thermal conductivity of the graphene ink is uncertain.

The resistance is where the twin pays for itself: 7 Ω simulated against 14 Ω measured. The model has no contact resistance, so the gap most likely is one: an ohmic interlayer or a different interconnect metal could double the power. The model also shows that most of the resistance sits in the thin silver interconnects, so making them thicker would raise the output by more than an order of magnitude.

04 · Compact thermal model

Why the textbook circuit fails

A full 3D simulation is accurate, but a designer also wants a compact model: a network of thermal resistances that can be solved by hand. The standard one for TEGs assumes the metal interconnects conduct heat so well that every leg sits at the same temperature. The FEA shows that in a thin printed device this is wrong. The interconnects are 4.5 mm long, 2 mm wide and only 3 µm thick, so their in-plane thermal resistance is large and the legs are thermally decoupled: each one develops its own temperature difference, through its own share of the substrate beneath it.

That is good news for a unipolar device: the p-type leg builds up a real ΔT regardless of the silver leg beside it. Under the standard model, heat would bypass the p-type legs through the silver and the device would barely produce a voltage. A compact circuit with decoupled legs predicts VOC as well as the full 3D simulation; the standard one falls far below the measurements.

Following the heat through one thermocouple

The FEA can be read anywhere, including inside layers no probe can reach. Move the slider, or drag on the cross-section, to climb through one thermocouple from the hot face of the substrate to the cold top contact: the marker moves to the same layer in the temperature map and on the profile along the graphene leg.

The graphene leg builds its own gradient, all of it inside the leg, while the silver leg beside it loses its whole temperature difference in the substrate. But even the graphene leg only gets what the substrate leaves behind: at the top of the substrate, 3.3 of the 25 K are left.

05 · Thermal management

Where the temperature difference goes

The profile above holds the biggest surprise: the substrate takes most of the temperature difference. It sits in series with the legs, so every kelvin it keeps is one the legs never see. A thinner substrate leaves more ΔT for the legs, and the gain is larger for thicker legs.

Against that ratio the nine curves fold onto one: neither thickness matters on its own, only how the substrate's thermal resistance compares with the legs'. A more conductive substrate works even better than a thinner one, because power scales with VOC2. Kapton grades at 0.8 W m-1 K-1 would multiply the power by ten. Commercial films above 30 W m-1 K-1, and flexible dielectrics reported up to 60, would give almost a hundredfold.

The dielectric: a path around the legs

The legs sit in wells of a printed dielectric, and heat can go around them through it, in parallel with the legs. Sweeping the dielectric's thermal conductivity in the model shows how much that path matters. The printed dielectric conducts 0.3 W m-1 K-1.

The rule is the opposite of the one for the substrate: the substrate should conduct heat as well as possible, the dielectric as poorly as possible. Neither layer shows up in a material's zT, and between them they decide how much of the temperature difference the legs get.

06 · Design-space exploration

Three orders of magnitude from geometry alone

With a validated model, the thickness of every component becomes a parameter to sweep, and each one controls a different property.

How far can this architecture go? Starting from the printed geometry, I simulated three material pairs. The first is the graphene / silver device as built. The second replaces silver with PBDFO, a scalable n-type polymer (zT 0.27). The third pairs PBDFO with PMHJ, the record p-type organic material (zT 0.74). Materials alone take the output from 0.1 to 0.5 and then 2.9 µW.

Then the design parameters change, one at a time:

  • Substrate: from 25 to 5 µm, at 0.8 W m-1 K-1, raises VOC more than fourfold.
  • Legs: from 15 to 50 µm, another ~10% of VOC.
  • Interconnects: from 3 to 25 µm thick, internal resistance divided by eight.
  • Interconnect material: bulk-silver conductivity brings it below 100 mΩ.

The projected output reaches 10 mW, a normalized power density of 10 µW cm-2 K-2. That is on par with commercial bismuth telluride modules, which are heavier, rigid and fragile, and take energy-intensive processing to make. The architecture matters more than the materials: as it improves, the device figure of merit ZT approaches the limit set by the materials' zT.

07 · System level

Heat still has to get in and out

These are estimates. At these voltages the currents would reach several amps, where Joule heating and the Peltier effect, which the model leaves out, would matter. More importantly, the optimised devices conduct heat so well that only an exceptional heat exchanger could keep their faces at the set temperatures. Fitting one would defeat the point of a low-cost harvester.

The better route is thermal impedance matching: choose the device's thickness so that its thermal resistance equals that of the heat exchangers around it. For this design the optimum is millimetres to centimetres thick, beyond what screen printing can lay down, so the practical answer is to stack several printed OTEGs. That system-level view is where the next chapter picks up.
